newsitem.title: GERMANY: Clarke - says G7 did not have in-depth talk on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Clarke - says G7 did not have in-depth talk on EMU.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Saturday that the Group of Seven nations did not discuss European Economic and Monetary Union EMU in any substatial way.

At a news conference, following the one-day meeting with his G7 counterparts, Clarke also said that the United States, Japan, and Canada did not initiate any discussion about the euro, European single currency.
"The first thing to make clear is we did not have a substantial discussion on EMU," Clarke said.
He said German Finance Minister Theo Waigel gave a report at the meeting on the Dublin summit of European leaders last year but beyond that, the subject of the planned single currency did not arise.
"The G7 just spent five hours together without discussing EMU or the euro, apart from Theo Waigel's report on the Dublin summit," Clarke said.
Asked whether there was any U.S. concern about the potential impact of the introduction of the euro, he said the United States, Japan and Canada had not even brought the subject up.
"It seems to me, the three non-Europeans felt no need to initiate a discussion (on the euro)," Clarke said.

The runup to the meeting was marked by controversy over EMU following a newspaper report, later denied by numerous officials, that there was a possibility of a deal for a late entry into EMU by Italy.
There had been some speculation in financial markets that non-European G7 authorities might want to ask the European finance ministers and central bankers first-hand about the EMU situation.
Clarke was asked about the state of the economies in Europe and whether the U.S. was concerned about the impact of Maastricht criteria on European growth levels.
"The key thing for all of us is to get unemployment to the lowest sustainable levels," he said, noting this was Britain's policy. And the key to that, he added, was to have flexible labour markets.
In terms of overall economic prospects, Clarke said "on the G7 themselves, the report from the managing director (of the IMF, Michel Camdessus) was that the prospect was relatively encouraging."
"As the British minister, I was very pleased that the American, British and Canadian economies really were creating no problems," he said.
Clarke reiterated the G7's position, contained in a brief statement issued after the meeting, that major misalignments in exchange markets as noted in an April 1995 communique had been corrected.
Bank of England governor Eddie George, who also attended the G7 meeting and was at the news conference, said there was no discussion of any particular ranges or levels of currencies.
"The judgments that were reached were pretty broad-brush," George said.
